claims.notes: HAP Table 1 and Table 3 row RR 2010b Appendix Table 1 give -0.1.

claims.passage: median growth rates for countries with public debt over roughly 90 percent of GDP are about one percent lower than otherwise; (mean) growth rates are several percent lower" (RR 2010a p. 573).

claims.passage: Title: Growth in a Time of Debt; Journal: American Economic Review; Vol. 100, No. 2; May 2010; pp. 573-78

claims.claim: By April 2013 the authors' website listed 76 high-profile media features
claims.passage: Reinhart's and Rogoff's website lists 76 high-profile features, including The Economist, Wall Street Journal ... (visited 7 April 2013.

claims.claim: Google Scholar returned 538 results citing it, excluding the authors' own
claims.passage: A search on [Reinhart Rogoff "Growth in a Time of Debt" -author:rogoff -author:reinhart] yielded 538 Google Scholar results on 7 April 2013).
claims.notes: Search excludes author:rogoff and author:reinhart; 'citing it' is a slight gloss on 'results'.

claims.claim: HAP reported it was the only evidence cited on debt and growth in the "Paul Ryan Budget", whose "Path to Prosperity" called it "conclusive empirical evidence" that debt over 90% "has a significant negative effect on economic growth."
claims.passage: RR 2010a is the only evidence cited in the "Paul Ryan Budget" on the consequences of high public debt for economic growth. ... The study found conclusive empirical evidence that gross debt ... exceeding 90 percent of the economy has a significant negative eect on economic growth. (Ryan 2013 p. 78)
claims.notes: Reported, not asserted, and attributed to HAP; the budget document itself was not fetched, which the disclosure states. 'eect' is a PDF ligature artifact.

claims.claim: HAP could not reproduce the result from the public data. The authors sent them the working spreadsheet.
claims.passage: We were unable to replicate the RR results from the publicly available country spreadsheet data ... Reinhart and Rogoff kindly provided us with the working spreadsheet from the RR analysis.
claims.notes: HAP add that their initial public-data results 'closely resemble' the corrected ones, which the body omits.

claims.claim: HAP got 2.2%.
claims.passage: With the working spreadsheet, we were able to approximate closely the published RR results. ... when properly calculated, the average real GDP growth rate ... is actually 2.2 percent, not -0.1 percent
claims.notes: 2.2 is HAP's corrected figure, but the sentence placement implies it came straight from the spreadsheet; they first approximated -0.1, then corrected.

claims.claim: Coding error: a formula averaged lines 30 to 44 instead of 30 to 49, dropping Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada and Denmark entirely
claims.passage: RR averaged cells in lines 30 to 44 instead of lines 30 to 49.  /  A coding error in the RR working spreadsheet entirely excludes five countries, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, and Denmark, from the analysis.
claims.notes: Matches HAP text and footnote 5; erratum confirms the same five countries.

claims.claim: "The omitted countries are selected alphabetically."
claims.passage: The omitted countries are selected alphabetically and, hence, likely randomly with respect to economic relationships.
claims.notes: Verbatim fragment.

claims.claim: Available early years were left out for Australia, Canada and New Zealand; NZ's excluded years grew 7.7, 11.9, -9.9 and 10.8 percent; remaining year 1951 at -7.6%
claims.passage: Real GDP growth rates in those years were 7.7, 11.9, -9.9, and 10.8 percent. After the exclusion of these years, New Zealand contributes only one year to the highest public debt/GDP category, 1951, with a real GDP growth rate of -7.6 percent.
claims.notes: Direct match.

claims.claim: Britain contributed 19 years averaging 2.4%; with 7 countries, NZ's 1 year carried 14.3% of the weight; transcription error moved it to -7.9%
claims.passage: the UK (19 years with average growth of 2.4 percent) ... a full 14.3 percent (one-seventh) ... An apparent transcription error ... reduced New Zealand's average growth ... from -7.6 to -7.9 percent per year.
claims.notes: Direct match.

claims.claim: The paper reported 96 country-years above 90%. HAP found 110. The calculation used 71.
claims.passage: RR reports 96 country-years in the highest public debt/GDP category. Our corrected analysis finds 110 ... RR in fact estimated GDP growth in the highest public debt/GDP category with only 71 country-years of data
claims.notes: Direct match.

claims.claim: Ledger: 'Corrected for any 1 of the 3 errors alone (HAP Table 3)' = 1.9%; body: 'HAP's Table 3 corrects the errors 1 at a time. Each alone moves the result 0.3 of a point, from 2.2% to 1.9%.'
claims.passage: Separate effects of RR calculations: Spreadsheet error only 4.2 3.0 3.2 1.9 / Selective years exclusion only 4.2 3.1 3.2 1.9 / Country weights only 4.0 3.0 3.0 1.9
claims.notes: 1.9 is the result of applying ONE RR error to correct data, not of correcting one error in the published figure; correcting one error from the published state gives 0.3 (spreadsheet), 1.4 (exclusion) or 1.7 (weights) per Table 3 rows, so label and 'corrects ... 1 at a time' misdescribe the table's direction.

claims.claim: Title: 'Each error cost 0.3 of a point'
claims.passage: Selective years exclusion only ... 1.9; Country weights only ... 1.9; Spreadsheet error only ... 1.9; ... Spreadsheet error + Selective years exclusion + Country weights 0.0; ... + Transcription error -0.1
claims.notes: True for the 3 standalone errors against the 2.2 baseline; the transcription error cost 0.1 and the marginal effects inside the full combination are 0.3, 1.4 and 1.7, so the unqualified title is order-dependent and invites a minimizing screenshot.

claims.claim: All 3 together take it to 0.0%. The transcription error supplies the last 0.1.
claims.passage: Spreadsheet error + Selective years exclusion + Country weights 4.1 2.9 3.4 0.0 ... Transcription error 4.1 2.9 3.4 -0.1
claims.notes: Table 3 and footnote 6 (-0.1 point).

claims.claim: Together the 3 cost 2.2 points, more than twice the sum of their parts
claims.passage: Some of the errors have strong interactive effects. ... Spreadsheet error + Selective years exclusion + Country weights ... 0.0
claims.notes: 2.2 - 0.0 = 2.2; sum of standalone effects = 0.9; 2.2 / 0.9 = 2.4, so 'more than twice' holds.

claims.claim: HAP: "Some of the errors have strong interactive effects."
claims.passage: Some of the errors have strong interactive effects.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: The spreadsheet error is the part that gets remembered, because the 5 countries it dropped were the first 5 in the alphabet.
claims.notes: No listed source says what gets remembered or why; an unsourced characterization of public memory (the erratum says only that the discussion focused on the >90% bucket).

claims.claim: The weighting amplified the exclusion, so that New Zealand's 1 remaining year, at -7.6%, carried a seventh of the result.
claims.passage: the impact of the excluded years for New Zealand is greatly amplified when equal country weighting assigns 14.3 percent (1/7) of the weight ... to the single year ... -7.6 percent.
claims.notes: Direct match.

claims.claim: Ledger: 'Corrected for all 3, plus a transcription slip' = 2.2%
claims.passage: Country-year weighting, all data  4.2   3.1  3.2  2.2
claims.notes: Table 3 corrected row.

claims.claim: Verdict: -0.1% became 2.2% in the replication, and 2.0% or 1.0% in the authors' own final correction, by NZ GDP series
claims.passage: Final including New Zealand (NZ Historical Statistics GDP) ... Post war Mean 4.2 3.0 2.4 2.0 ... Final including New Zealand (Maddison GDP) ... Post war Mean 4.2 3.0 2.5 1.0
claims.notes: Postwar mean above 90% is 2.0 and 1.0; resolves the prior omission of the final panels.

claims.passage: The authors wish to thank Thomas Herndon, Michael Ash, and Robert Pollin (HAP) for the careful attention and for pointing out an important correction to our original Growth in a Time of Debt.

claims.passage: (i) a coding error that causes the first five countries in the alphabet to be omitted in forming averages for the 1946-2009 period in one figure
claims.notes: Erratum states this as HAP's assertion and then confirms the coding error in 'Guide to changes'; the body presents it as the erratum's own fix, which the later section supports.

claims.claim: Erratum adds missing years for Spain, includes NZ's 1948 and 1949 as "a coding correction", adds a second NZ GDP series beside the Maddison series
claims.passage: First, a coding correction that includes 1948, 1949 in the postwar sample ... Second, the GDP growth series was itself replaced. ... We also retain the Maddison series.
claims.notes: Matches; Spain 1959-1980 years added.

claims.passage: Their paper is silent on the results of the longer sample dating back to the 1800s for most of the advanced economies and the exercise on emerging markets
claims.notes: Reported as the erratum's claim; HAP's own text says it replicates only the first sample, which is consistent.

claims.claim: HAP "fails to mention that our median estimates for the postwar sample are very close in magnitude to the averages that they present."
claims.passage: It also fails to mention that our median estimates for the postwar sample are very close in magnitude to the averages that they present.
claims.notes: Quote verbatim, presented as the erratum's statement; the erratum's final postwar medians are 2.5 and 1.9.

claims.claim: The erratum disputes the rest
claims.passage: (ii) "selective exclusion" of 1946-1950 for New Zealand, and (iii) "unconventional weighting of summary statistics." ... A major shortcoming of the HAP paper is thatthat it ignores entirely the rapidly expanding post-May 2010 academic literature
claims.notes: Erratum puts exclusion and weighting in scare quotes and does not concede them, but also says it 'fully agree[s] with much of the HAP commentary' on volatile postwar growth; 'disputes the rest' is a fair but compressed reading.
